**Abstract**

Extreme heat events are becoming more frequent, intense and prolonged, making it urgent to predict how heat intensity and exposure duration combine to threaten organisms. Thermal death time (TDT) and thermal load sensitivity (TLS) models provide this link, but conventional two-stage analyses often discard uncertainty, mishandle censored or overdispersed data and limit inference. We show how hierarchical dose-response models can be reparameterized to recover TDT/TLS quantities, including thermal tolerance ($CT_{max}$), sensitivity ($z$), critical temperature ($T_{crit}$), heat injury and survival, from one model. Simulations show the joint model reproduces classical estimates when two-stage assumptions hold and is more reliable when they fail. We introduce Bayesian and frequentist R packages to implement these workflows. Case studies across plant and animal taxa show this framework can estimate group contrasts and predict survival from realistic field temperature-time series. This framework provides more robust inference and flexible tools for predicting organismal responses to extreme heat events.

**Keywords:** thermal tolerance landscape; dose-response; hierarchical Bayesian model; 4-parameter log-logistic; critical thermal maximum; ectotherm; heat tolerance; climate change; climate vulnerability; fluctuating temperature regimes; bayesTLS; freqTLS
:::

```{r}
# Used for inline reporting so headline numbers are produced by code, not typed.

fig4_summary <- readRDS(here::here("output", "data", "fig4_summary.rds"))

# Zebrafish oxygen contrast (OCLTT): CTmax_1hr under normoxia vs hyperoxia.
.zf_ct <- fig4_summary[fig4_summary$case_study == "Zebrafish (oxygen)" &
                       fig4_summary$quantity == "CTmax_1hr", ]
zf_ctmax_norm  <- round(.zf_ct$median[.zf_ct$group == "normoxia"], 1)
zf_ctmax_hyper <- round(.zf_ct$median[.zf_ct$group == "hyperoxia"], 1)

# Per-group medians underlying the case-study contrasts highlighted in the text
# (all from the same fig4_summary build; produced by code, not typed). f1()
# formats to one decimal so paired values read consistently (e.g. 44.0 not 44).
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
g4 <- function(cs, grp, q)
  fig4_summary$median[fig4_summary$case_study == cs &
                      fig4_summary$group == grp &
                      fig4_summary$quantity == q]
# Same lookup, formatted as "median [lo, hi]" (1 dp) for inline group reporting
# with 95% credible intervals (used where we want to emphasise uncertainty).
g4ci <- function(cs, grp, q) {
  r <- fig4_summary[fig4_summary$case_study == cs &
                    fig4_summary$group == grp &
                    fig4_summary$quantity == q, ]
  sprintf("%.1f [%.1f, %.1f]", r$median, r$lower, r$upper)
}
# Cereal aphids: least-sensitive (highest z) and most-tolerant (highest CTmax).
aphid_z_md  <- f1(g4("Cereal aphids", "M_dirhodum", "z"))
aphid_ct_rp <- f1(g4("Cereal aphids", "R_padi",     "CTmax_1hr"))
# Vinegar fly: sex-specific mortality z and CTmax_4hr.
fly_z_f   <- f1(g4("Vinegar fly (mortality)", "Female", "z"))
fly_z_m   <- f1(g4("Vinegar fly (mortality)", "Male",   "z"))
fly_ct_4h <- f1(g4("Vinegar fly (mortality)", "Female", "CTmax_4hr"))

fly_z_f_ci     <- g4ci("Vinegar fly (mortality)", "Female", "z")
fly_z_m_ci     <- g4ci("Vinegar fly (mortality)", "Male",   "z")

zf_ct_hyper_ci <- g4ci("Zebrafish (oxygen)", "hyperoxia", "CTmax_1hr")

# Calibrated case-study CONTRASTS + the repair effect, produced by the

cc <- readRDS(here::here("output", "data", "case_study_contrasts.rds"))
# Display helpers: signed "x [lo, hi]", positive-magnitude version, pMCMC string, repair %.
ci1  <- function(v) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f, %.1f]", v["med"], v["lo"], v["hi"])
ci1a <- function(v) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f, %.1f]", abs(v["med"]), min(abs(v[c("lo", "hi")])), max(abs(v[c("lo", "hi")])))
pmc  <- function(v) if (v["p"] < 1e-3) "$p_{\\mathrm{MCMC}}$ < .001" else paste0("$p_{\\mathrm{MCMC}}$ = ", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", v["p"])))
# Repair effect as "med [lo, hi]" percentage points. Whole-number rounding is too
# coarse here: it collapsed R. padi's lower bound (0.28) to 0 and printed
# M. dirhodum's ~7e-6% effect as "0 [0, 0]", implying an exact zero. When the
# entire interval falls below the display resolution, report a single "< limit".
rep1 <- function(v, digits = 1) {
  lim <- 10^(-digits)
  if (v["hi"] < lim) return(sprintf(paste0("< %.", digits, "f"), lim))
  f <- paste0("%.", digits, "f")
  sprintf(paste0(f, " [", f, ", ", f, "]"), v["med"], v["lo"], v["hi"])
}

  v <- unique(vapply(fits, function(x)

    character(1)))
  paste(format(sort(numeric_version(v))), collapse = " and ")
})
```

# Introduction

Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme heat events globally, with cascading consequences for organismal fitness, population persistence, and biodiversity [@snook_fertility_2026; @arnold_thermal_2025; @rezende_drosophila_mortality_2020; @smale_marine_2019; @wiens_localextinctions_2016]. Quantifying variation in thermal tolerance within and among species is central to forecasting biological responses to climate change in nature [@sunday_global_2011; @deutsch_latitude_2008; @sunday_redistribution_2012; @pinsky_marine_2019; @jorgensen_nature_2022; @duarte; @comte2017]. Threshold-based measures of heat tolerance, such as the critical thermal maximum ($CT_{max}$), have long been used to understand differences in sensitivity among taxa and to predict vulnerability to climate change [@pottier_amphibians_2025; @sunday_global_2011; @deutsch_latitude_2008; @sunday_redistribution_2012; @pinsky_marine_2019]. While useful for comparisons, threshold-based metrics do not capture how the biological effects of heat stress on fitness depend on both exposure duration and intensity, limiting our ability to make realistic predictions in nature [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @orsted_finding_2022; @jorgensen_unifying_2021; @clusella-trullas2021; @troia2023].

The Thermal Death Time (TDT) and Thermal Load Sensitivity (TLS) frameworks address this limitation by quantifying how the intensity and duration of heat exposure jointly determine survival and other fitness-related responses [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @orsted_finding_2022; @jorgensen_nature_2022; @jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @arnold_thermal_2025; @cook_cumulative_plants_2024]. Recent extensions apply the same logic to sublethal endpoints, such as sterility and heat coma [@orsted_suzukii_2024; @arnold_thermal_2025; @vanheerwaarden2021]. These models describe heat injury as a dose-dependent process above a critical threshold ($T_{crit}$). Thermal injury accumulates more rapidly at higher temperatures and during longer exposures, and organisms may eventually reach a thermal load that compromises growth, reproduction, or survival if injury cannot be repaired [@orsted_finding_2022; @rezende_landscapes_2014; @arnold_thermal_2025; @jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @buckley_damage_2025; @jorgensen_unifying_2021]. By linking biological responses to the intensity and duration of heat stress, TDT/TLS frameworks allow more realistic predictions under fluctuating thermal regimes [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @orsted_finding_2022; @jorgensen_unifying_2021], and have shown promise in predicting observed mortality rates in nature [@rezende_drosophila_mortality_2020; @zamora2026; @verberk2023; @molina2025].

Despite their potential predictive power, TDT/TLS analyses traditionally involve a two-stage modelling approach [@orsted_finding_2022; @rezende_drosophila_mortality_2020; @truebano2018; @jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @li2023]. First, organisms are exposed to multiple temperatures for different durations, and the proportion of individuals that are dead, infertile, knocked down, or otherwise impaired or affected is modelled as a function of exposure duration. This is typically done by fitting independent dose-response curves at each assay temperature ([@fig-joint-4pl-conceptual]a). From these curves, the exposure duration required to reach a specified response threshold is estimated, most often $t_{50}$, the time required to reach 50% mortality, infertility, knockdown, or some other endpoint. Second, the resulting $\log_{10}(t_{50})$ estimates are regressed against assay temperature using linear regression. Thermal sensitivity ($z$), the temperature increase required to reduce $t_{50}$ by a factor of 10, and critical thermal maxima ($CT_{max_t}$) are then derived from this linear model [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @orsted_finding_2022] ([@fig-joint-4pl-conceptual]b). Because $CT_{max_t}$ is estimated at a fixed exposure duration, it corresponds to the static critical thermal maximum, often denoted $sCT_{max}$, in TDT/TLS studies [@jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @orsted_finding_2022]. We use $CT_{max}$ throughout for brevity. $CT_{max_t}$ is usually computed for a 1-min [@rezende_landscapes_2014], 1-hour [@jorgensen_drosophila_2019], or 4-hour [@orsted_suzukii_2024] duration of heat stress exposure. These quantities can then be used to estimate cumulative Heat Injury (HI) under natural temperatures, where injury is assumed to accumulate additively as a function of the exposure duration relative to the predicted tolerance time at each temperature [@jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @villeneuve_dynamic_2024]. Recent extensions have emphasized that injury accumulation may also be offset by repair or acclimation mechanisms, motivating the emergence of new models that incorporate damage-repair dynamics, although applying such approaches remains challenging [@arnold_thermal_2025; @buckley_damage_2025; @orsted2026; @wehrli2024; @schow-madsen2025].

While the two-stage pipeline is intuitive and easy to implement, it has several practical and statistical limitations [for a recent discussion of some issues, see @bullard2026]. First, it rarely propagates uncertainty. The $t_{50}$ estimates derived in the first stage have non-negligible sampling variance, but they are commonly treated as fixed-point estimates in the second-stage regression. Neglecting this sampling variance can bias or miscalibrate inference on $z$ and $CT_{max}$, and lead to inflated $R^2$ values. Second, models estimating $t_{50}$ often assume that upper and lower survival are 1 and 0, respectively. When data are sparse or do not span the response range, $t_{50}$ estimates can be biased or undefined, leading to inaccurate $z$ and $CT_{max}$ estimates. Third, group comparisons between species, sexes, or life stages inherit miscalibrated uncertainty [as discussed by @lappi2018], which affects inferences. Reducing each dose-response curve to a fixed $t_{50}$ estimate also makes it difficult to determine which aspects of the dose-response curve are affected. Fourth, fitting separate dose-response models for each assay temperature assumes that these estimates are independent, and typically ignores the hierarchical structure of experimental data. Ignoring this nesting structure prevents the decomposition of variance and can lead to pseudoreplication, particularly when replicate-level variation affects the shape or position of the dose-response curve [@hurlbert_1984; @schielzeth_nested_2013]. Finally, the two-stage pipeline does not easily allow downstream predictions of heat injury and survival in nature with uncertainty, which is key to inferring confidence in predictions of extreme-heat impacts.

Here, we present a single-stage alternative to the classical two-stage pipeline: a hierarchical log-logistic model fitted jointly to all temperature-by-duration response data. We show such a model can be reparameterised to capture classical TDT/TLS quantities, such as thermal sensitivity ($z$), thermal tolerance ($CT_{max}$), and critical temperature thresholds ($T_{crit}$). Heat injury accumulation, survival under fluctuating thermal regimes, and their uncertainty can then be derived from these critical parameters. To make the modelling approach accessible across the community, we develop these tools as two R packages, `bayesTLS` (Bayesian) and `freqTLS` (frequentist). We use simulations and empirical case studies across plant and animal taxa to demonstrate how to implement, validate, and extend this modelling framework. We then discuss how our reparameterised single-stage dose-response model opens up completely new opportunities for addressing exciting biological questions about thermal tolerance and sensitivity within and across species that have not been possible before.

# A non-linear hierarchical dose-response model for characterizing thermal load sensitivity


## Model specification

Our model builds on recent work by @bullard2026, who use log-logistic survival curves to examine how temperature-dependent variation in failure times affects survival predictions under fluctuating temperatures. Their increasing-variance prediction workflow fits curves separately at each temperature, then relates the fitted scale and shape parameters to temperature. While we use a similar dose-response model, our model differs in a number of significant ways. First, all dose-response models are fit in a single joint model. Second, we re-parameterise our model around $z$ and $CT_{max}$, which allows linear predictors to be placed directly on these estimates. Finally, our model makes it easier to propagate uncertainty, making inferences more robust.

To demonstrate our approach, assume we have mortality data at different times and temperatures, let $y$ denote the number of survivors among $n$ individuals exposed for time $t$ (e.g., minutes) at assay temperature $T$ (°C). We can model the counts directly with a binomial (or beta-binomial) likelihood:

$$
y \mid n, p \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}(n,\, p),
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

For demonstration purposes, we model survival probability $p$ using a four-parameter log-logistic (4PL) function of $\log_{10}$-exposure time:

$$
p \;=\; \text{low} \;+\; \frac{\text{up} - \text{low}}{1 + \exp\!\bigl(k\,(\log_{10} t - \text{mid})\bigr)}.
$$ {#eq-4pl}

where $\text{low}$ is the lower survival probability asymptote, $\text{up}$ is the upper survival probability asymptote, and $k$ is the steepness parameter controlling how rapidly survival probability declines on the $\log_{10} t$ axis (the slope of $p$ versus $\log_{10} t$ at the midpoint is $-k(\text{up} - \text{low})/4$). Larger $k$ gives a sharper decline in survival probability with $\log_{10} t$. $\text{mid}$ is the value of $\log_{10} t$ at which $p$ falls to the midpoint between $\text{low}$ and $\text{up}$. 

We use the log-logistic function to demonstrate our approach because its midpoint is the time by which half the responding animals have died, which is the LT50, the measure used in classical TDT theory (see below). Additionally, the log-logistic model is widely used in the dose-response literature [@ritz_ecotox_2010], and has been shown to be a better or equally supported model for heat knockdown times in most of the *Drosophila* species tested [@bullard2026]. As will become clear, we focus on the four-parameter log-logistic (rather than the two- or three-parameter log-logistic) because it provides a flexible sigmoidal description of thermal dose responses, with interpretable parameters for the lower asymptote, upper asymptote, curve steepness, and midpoint [@ritz_drc_2015; @ritz_ecotox_2010; @nielsen_nlmm_2004; @rudemo_random_1989; @ritz_streibig_2008]. @bullard2026 already show that it is important to consider temperature effects on $k$, and we show in our simulations that when different parts of the dose-response curve vary with temperature (e.g., $k$, $\text{up}$), it can impact inferences. As such, we recommend fitting a four-parameter model initially and simplifying when needed. For simplicity, we also focus on binomial and beta-binomial outcomes because count data dominate TDT/TLS studies, but the same modelling logic can be extended to other response types using appropriate likelihoods, including continuous performance traits or latency data.


# Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters

The TDT/TLS frameworks are elegant in that they derive metrics with clear biological interpretation that can be compared across populations and species (e.g., *z*, $CT_{max_{1hr}}$). Here, we show that we can derive these same metrics directly from @eq-4pl.

As indicated above, we can model changes in the mean of any of the four parameters in @eq-4pl. Thermal sensitivity (*z*) and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ can be derived by modelling the effect of temperature on midpoints specifically ([@fig-joint-4pl-conceptual]b), as follows:

$$
\text{mid} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,(T - \bar{T}),
$$ {#eq-mid-temp}

where $\text{mid}$ is the $\log_{10}$-time at which survival equals the midpoint between the lower and upper asymptotes at assay temperature $T$ (°C); $\beta_0$ is the intercept giving the midpoint at the grand mean temperature $\bar{T}$; $\beta_1$ is the slope describing how the midpoint changes per °C increase in $T$; and $\bar{T}$ is the grand mean of assay temperatures used to mean-centre $T$, which decorrelates $\beta_0$ from $\beta_1$ and improves parameter estimation and interpretation [@schielzeth_centering_2010].

When the experimental design estimates lower and upper limits of the response (i.e., $\text{low}$ and $\text{up}$) near 0 and 1, the 4PL midpoint is close to the classical $t_{50}$. The two are identical whenever $\text{low} + \text{up} = 1$, because survival at the midpoint, $(\text{low} + \text{up})/2$, is then exactly 50%. When $\text{low} = 0$ and $\text{up} = 1$, @eq-4pl also gives the log-logistic survival function used by @bullard2026, with scale $10^{\text{mid}}$ and shape $k/\ln 10$. However, @bullard2026 estimate the temperature dependence of scale and shape in two stages, which our model circumvents. When $\text{low}$ and $\text{up}$ are fixed at 0 and 1, @eq-mid-temp directly gives $z = -1/\beta_1$, and the critical thermal limit at any reference time $t_\text{ref}$ is $CT_{max}(t_\text{ref}) = \bar{T} + (\log_{10} t_\text{ref} - \beta_0)/\beta_1$ (with $t_\text{ref} = 60$ min for $CT_{max_{1hr}}$).

More generally, the 4PL distinguishes between two related threshold definitions ([@fig-joint-4pl-conceptual]b). A *relative* threshold is defined by each curve's own midpoint, $p = (\text{up}+\text{low})/2$. On this scale, $\text{mid}(T)$ is exactly the relative $\log_{10}t_{50}$, so $z_\text{rel} = -1/\beta_1$ and $CT_{max,\text{rel}}$ is read directly from @eq-mid-temp. An *absolute* threshold instead asks when survival reaches a fixed probability, such as 50% survival, regardless of the fitted asymptotes. When the $\text{low}$ and $\text{up}$ asymptotes do not sum to 1 (e.g., $\text{low} = 0$ but $\text{up} < 1$), this absolute threshold no longer coincides with the midpoint and requires an asymmetry correction (see [Supplement Section 17](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-ms-derive)):

$$
\log_{10} t_{50}(T) \;=\; \text{mid}(T) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{k}\ln\!\left(\tfrac{\text{up} - 0.5}{0.5 - \text{low}}\right),
$$ {#eq-t50}

The corresponding absolute $CT_{max}$ is obtained by applying the same correction on the temperature scale:

$$
CT_{max}(t_\text{ref}) \;=\; \bar{T} + \frac{\log_{10} t_\text{ref} - \beta_0}{\beta_1} \;-\; \frac{1}{\beta_1}\cdot\tfrac{1}{k}\ln\!\left(\tfrac{\text{up} - 0.5}{0.5 - \text{low}}\right).
$$ {#eq-ctmax-corrected}

This distinction matters most when asymptotes or curve steepness vary with temperature. If the correction is constant across temperatures, absolute and relative $z$ are the same, although $CT_{max}$ may shift. If the correction changes with temperature, absolute $\log_{10}t_{50}$ is no longer parallel to the midpoint line, and $z_\text{abs}$ can differ from $z_\text{rel}$.

The same logic applies to any fixed mortality threshold. For example, $\log_{10}t_{10}(T)$ is the time to 10% mortality (90% survival) and can identify the onset of population-level mortality, whereas $\log_{10}t_{90}(T)$ is the time to 90% mortality (10% survival) and is closer to population collapse. Any mortality threshold can be estimated by using the corresponding probability in the correction term:

$$
\log_{10} t_m(T) \;=\; \text{mid}(T) \;+\; \frac{1}{k}\,\ln\!\left(\frac{\text{up} - (1-m/100)}{(1-m/100) - \text{low}}\right),
$$ {#eq-LTx}

Here, $m$ is the mortality percentage and $1-m/100$ is the corresponding survival probability. Relative thresholds are useful when differences in asymptotes reflect baseline survival or incomplete response ranges. In contrast, absolute thresholds are useful when the biological question concerns a fixed survival or mortality probability. We therefore recommend reporting which threshold definition was used and, where asymptotes differ strongly among groups or temperatures, checking whether conclusions change under both definitions. In practice, there will often be little difference between relative and absolute summaries (i.e., *z* and $CT_{max}$), but this distinction is important nonetheless.

Equivalently, the model can be reparameterised to estimate *z* and $CT_{max}$ directly. Inverting the relations above ($\beta_1 = -1/z$ and $\beta_0 = \log_{10} t_\text{ref} + (CT_{max} - \bar{T})/z$) reparameterises the midpoint as $\text{mid}(T) = \log_{10} t_\text{ref} + \bigl(CT_{max}(t_\text{ref}) - T\bigr)/z$, which substituted into @eq-4pl gives

$$
p \;=\; \text{low} \;+\; \frac{\text{up} - \text{low}}{1 + \exp\!\left(k\,\left[\log_{10} t - \log_{10} t_\text{ref} - \tfrac{CT_{max}(t_\text{ref}) - T}{z}\right]\right)}.
$$ {#eq-4pl-direct}

Now *z* (estimated on the log scale so it stays positive) and $CT_{max}$ are estimated parameters in their own right, rather than quantities recovered from @eq-mid-temp after fitting. @eq-4pl-direct uses the relative threshold (each curve's own midpoint); an absolute threshold is obtained by adding the midpoint-scale asymmetry correction of @eq-t50, $\frac{1}{k}\ln\!\left(\frac{\text{up} - 0.5}{0.5 - \text{low}}\right)$, to $\text{mid}(T)$ before solving for $CT_{max}$. Again, temperature effects (and any interactions with moderators) should be included on $\text{low}$, $\text{up}$, and $k$ initially to correctly estimate absolute thresholds, whereas relative thresholds depend only on $\text{mid}(T)$. These connections apply to any dose-response curve with a parameter that sets its position along the time axis, including log-logistic, Gompertz and Weibull curves ([Supplement Section 5](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-alt-kernels)). The log-logistic is easiest to explain because its midpoint corresponds directly to $t_{50}$ when survival ranges from 1 to 0. 

A powerful aspect of the modelling approach described above is that uncertainty in all estimated quantities can be carried through the full analysis. The direct parameterisation (@eq-4pl-direct) opens up exciting new ways of modelling *z* and $CT_{max}$ that the two-stage approach cannot, while ensuring correct error propagation and inference. Each parameter in the model — `low`, `up`, `k`, `mid`, and, under @eq-4pl-direct, *z* and $CT_{max}$ — can be estimated separately for biologically meaningful strata (e.g., sex, population, species, treatment) by adding covariates and, where appropriate, random effects to the relevant parameter predictors (see @eq-empirical-direct below). This makes *a priori* tests of key hypotheses (e.g., do sexes or species differ significantly in *z* and $CT_{max}$?) and variance decomposition (e.g., how much variation in *z* and $CT_{max}$ arises across populations, species, or trials?) part of the model rather than a post-hoc comparison of fitted curves, all with correct inference. We fit the examples below in a Bayesian framework because posterior draws make uncertainty propagation straightforward, but the same likelihoods can also be fit in a frequentist framework, with uncertainty propagated by profiled likelihoods, the Delta method, or parametric bootstrap.

# Predicting heat injury and survival under dynamic thermal environments

A particularly powerful aspect of TDT/TLS models are their ability to translate dynamic temperature time series from nature to predict heat injury (HI) accumulation and thus population survival probability [@jorgensen_unifying_2021; @orsted_suzukii_2024; @li2023; @orsted_finding_2022; @rezende_drosophila_mortality_2020]. Heat injury accumulates as the time spent at a given temperature divided by the median lethal time at that temperature, integrated across the temperature trajectory $T(i)$ as follows:

$$
HI(t) \;=\; 100 \int_0^t 10^{\,\big(T(i)\,-\,CT_{max_{1hr}}\big)/z} \,di,
$$ {#eq-hi}

where $z$ describes thermal sensitivity and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ is the static temperature at which 50% of the population reaches the assayed endpoint after one hour of exposure. Larger $z$ values indicate that a larger temperature increase is needed to reduce tolerance time by a factor of 10, so they correspond to lower sensitivity of tolerance time to warming. When $HI(t) = 100\%$, the cumulative dose equals one $t_{50}$ at the 1-hour reference, predicting 50% mortality (or 50% loss of the assayed sublethal endpoint, e.g.\ fertility; @orsted_suzukii_2024). Injury accumulates only when $T(i)$ exceeds a critical temperature $T_{crit}$ below which damage is repaired as fast as it accrues [@jorgensen_unifying_2021; @orsted_finding_2022].

A more natural prediction to make may instead be the population-level survival probability over time [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @rezende_drosophila_mortality_2020]. This has the advantage of allowing for a direct connection to population dynamical models which typically use survival, growth and fecundity as vital rates for population-level predictions [@noble2026]. To predict survival, we can calculate the *effective exposure time* at a chosen reference temperature $T_{\text{ref}}$. More effective exposure time is accumulated at higher temperatures and less at cool ones, in proportion to the scaling factor $10^{(T(i) - T_{\text{ref}})/z}$,

$$
\tau_{\text{eff}}(t) \;=\; \int_0^t 10^{\,(T(i) - T_{\text{ref}})/z}\,di,
$$ {#eq-tau-eff}

We can then evaluate the 4PL surface once at the cumulative effective exposure to obtain the predicted population-level survival fraction at every point in the trajectory:

$$
S_{\text{pred}}(t) \;=\; S\!\big(T_{\text{ref}},\, \tau_{\text{eff}}(t)\big).
$$ {#eq-S-pred}

Here $S(T, \tau)$ is the survival surface fitted by the dose-response model, so $S_{\text{pred}}(t)$ is the survival probability for an organism held at *constant* $T_{\text{ref}}$ after exposure duration $\tau_{\text{eff}}(t)$. Direct error propagation of $z$ and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ (using either Bayesian or frequentist approaches) allows one to easily model variation in outcomes, which can be helpful in making informed predictions in nature.

# Simulations - Evaluating statistical properties of the joint and two-stage modelling approaches

We assessed the performance of both the 4PL and two-stage approaches by estimating bias and 95% coverage for *z* and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ across simulation replicates. Bias was calculated as the estimated value minus the true value, whereas coverage was defined as the proportion of intervals containing the true parameter value. The 4PL approach estimated parameter uncertainty directly from the fitted model. In contrast, the two-stage approach required uncertainty to be propagated from the Stage-2 linear model using the Delta method, a first-order Taylor approximation for nonlinear functions of estimated parameters [@bolker_ecologicalmodels_2008; @lappi2018]. For the two-stage estimates, we constructed intervals using both normal and *t*-distribution quantiles to evaluate the sensitivity of coverage to different assumptions about sampling uncertainty.

We tested the performance of the two-stage and 4PL approaches across scenarios designed to separate different sources of estimator bias and uncertainty. First, we simulated a strict-equivalence baseline in which survival spanned the full 0–1 range, there was no overdispersion, and only the dose-response midpoint varied with temperature. This scenario tested whether the two approaches recover the same quantities when the assumptions of the classical two-stage model are met. Second, we introduced beta-binomial overdispersion while keeping the same underlying dose-response shape, allowing us to isolate the cost of likelihood misspecification when binomial models are applied to overdispersed count data. Third, we simulated departures from the classical dose-response assumptions by allowing the upper asymptote to decline with temperature, both asymptotes to compress with temperature, or the curve steepness to change with temperature. These scenarios reflect empirical cases in which survival or sublethal responses do not span the full response range, or where the shape of the dose-response curve changes across assay temperatures [e.g., @bullard2026]. We also ran sensitivity analyses that varied the strength of the upper-asymptote shift and the overall level of the upper asymptote.

Finally, we evaluated how different experimental designs impact estimates by simulating response curves from several static temperatures and exposure durations with modest numbers of individuals, samples, or replicate vials per treatment [@truebano2018; @jorgensen_drosophila_2019; @li2023; @orsted_suzukii_2024; @faber_tdt_plants_2024]. In the simulations, designs included 1, 3, or 5 replicate vials per temperature-by-time treatment, with 10 to 20 organisms per vial sampled from a uniform distribution. We also explored experimental designs that conducted experiments over short time spans across the different temperatures which we expected should impact model fit and therefore *z* and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$. For each scenario-by-design combination, we simulated 1,000 datasets and fitted both the two-stage and 4PL approaches, summarising the 4PL at both relative and absolute thresholds (at the absolute threshold, posterior draws with no crossing of the reference exposure were left out, as `tls()` does; [Supplement 13](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-extendsims)). Overall, this amounted to 29,000 simulations across the 29 scenario-by-design combinations. We report Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE) for the bias and coverage summaries to better understand across simulation uncertainty [@williams2024; @direnzo2023; @koehler2009].

#### *Simulation results*

When the data-generating process matched the classical assumptions, with survival spanning the full 0–1 range and temperature affecting only the dose-response midpoint, the two-stage approach performed similarly to the joint 4PL model, producing little bias and near-nominal coverage when confidence intervals were constructed with *t*-distribution quantiles. Using normal (z) quantiles instead produced anti-conservative intervals with coverage well below the nominal 95% level ([Supplement 13.1](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#strict-equivalence-baseline) and [13.2](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#likelihood-misspecification-alone)).

```{r}
#| label: sim-design-facts
#| echo: false
#| cache: false
# Inline facts for the experimental-design sentences below (scen8 = grid x
# replication, scen9 = maximum exposure), from the same per-simulation files,
# Stage-1 screening and truths as the fig-sim-design chunk. Inline code runs
# before that chunk, so it cannot reuse the chunk's objects.
.sd_ps <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(list.files(here::here("output", "sim_twostage"),
  pattern = "^per_sim_scen[89]_.*[.]rds$", full.names = TRUE), readRDS))
.sd_bad <- .sd_ps |>
  dplyr::filter(method == "two_stage_bb",
                (quantity == "z" & abs(bias) > 20) | (quantity == "CTmax_1hr" & abs(bias) > 10)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(scenario, sim_id) |>
  dplyr::mutate(bb_path = TRUE)
.sd_truth_rel <- c(z = -1 / -0.15, CTmax_1hr = 34 + (log10(60) - 1.5) / -0.15)
.sd_cell <- .sd_ps |>
  dplyr::left_join(.sd_bad, by = c("scenario", "sim_id")) |>
  dplyr::filter(success, is.na(bb_path) | !(method %in% c("two_stage_bb", "two_stage_bb_t"))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(truth_use = ifelse(method == "joint_4pl", .sd_truth_rel[as.character(quantity)], truth),
                covered = is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper) & lower <= truth_use & truth_use <= upper) |>
  dplyr::group_by(scenario, method, quantity) |>
  dplyr::summarise(coverage = mean(covered), width = stats::median(upper - lower), .groups = "drop")
rm(.sd_ps, .sd_bad)
# Range as "lo–hi" (a single value if both ends round the same).
.sd_rng <- function(x, fmt = "%.2f") paste(unique(sprintf(fmt, range(x))), collapse = "–")
.sd_joint  <- c("joint_4pl", "joint_4pl_abs")
.sd_tci    <- c("two_stage_bin_t", "two_stage_bb_t")
.sd_sparse <- dplyr::filter(.sd_cell, grepl("sparse", scenario))
# Joint 4PL coverage over every design cell (both thresholds, z and CTmax).
sim_joint_cov_rng <- .sd_rng(.sd_cell$coverage[.sd_cell$method %in% .sd_joint])
# Two-stage t-CI coverage on the sparse grids, and how many times wider its
# median interval is there than the joint 4PL's (same cell and quantity).
sim_sparse_tcov_rng <- .sd_rng(.sd_sparse$coverage[.sd_sparse$method %in% .sd_tci])
sim_sparse_wratio_rng <- .sd_sparse |>
  dplyr::group_by(scenario, quantity) |>
  dplyr::summarise(lo = min(width[method %in% .sd_tci]) / max(width[method %in% .sd_joint]),
                   hi = max(width[method %in% .sd_tci]) / min(width[method %in% .sd_joint]),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  with(.sd_rng(c(lo, hi), "%.0f"))
# Two-stage t-CI coverage of CTmax on the full grid with 3 or 5 replicates.
sim_ct_full_tcov_rng <- .sd_rng(.sd_cell$coverage[.sd_cell$scenario %in% c("scen8_full_n3", "scen8_full_n5") &
                                                  .sd_cell$quantity == "CTmax_1hr" &
                                                  .sd_cell$method %in% .sd_tci])
# Two-stage t-CI coverage of z at the shortest exposure cap (60 min).
sim_z60_tcov_rng <- .sd_rng(.sd_cell$coverage[.sd_cell$scenario == "scen9_tmax_060" &
                                              .sd_cell$quantity == "z" &
                                              .sd_cell$method %in% .sd_tci])
```

In contrast, the two-stage approach resulted in biased *z* and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$, often with poor coverage, when temperature affected the upper asymptote (`up`) or the rate of decline (`k`) (@fig-sims). Bias for both *z* and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ from the two-stage approaches was particularly severe as the upper survival threshold differed from 1, or decreased with temperature (@fig-sims2). These biases were consistent even with larger sample sizes ([Supplement 13.6](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#experimental-design-impacts)), but they became most consequential under exactly the types of experimental designs used in practice: sparse temperature-duration grids, short exposure windows, and low replication (@fig-sim-design). The joint 4PL remained less biased than the two-stage approach across these designs, with coverage close to nominal throughout (`r sim_joint_cov_rng`). Two-stage bias was larger on sparse compared to full grids, and larger at the two shortest exposure caps (60 and 120 min) than at the longer ones. With the *t*-correction, two-stage coverage was close to nominal on sparse grids (`r sim_sparse_tcov_rng`), but with intervals `r sim_sparse_wratio_rng` times wider than the joint 4PL's, and its coverage of $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ fell below nominal on the full grid with three or five replicates (`r sim_ct_full_tcov_rng`). At the two shortest exposure caps, two-stage coverage of *z* fell sharply even with the *t*-correction, to `r sim_z60_tcov_rng` at 60 min (@fig-sim-design; full per-cell detail in [Supplement 13.6](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#experimental-design-impacts)).

```{r}
#| label: fig-sims
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Simulation performance when the data-generating process violates classical TDT shape assumptions. Row labelled 'up varies with T': upper asymptote $\\text{up}$ declines 0.01 per °C from 0.92 at $T=34$ °C, with $\\text{low}=0.05$ and $k=8$ constant in $T$. Row labelled 'k varies with T': slope $k$ ranges from 7 at 30 °C to 9 at 38 °C, with $\\text{up}=0.92$ and $\\text{low}=0.05$ constant. Both rows use 5 replicate vials per (T × duration) cell, $N_{sim}=1000$ simulated datasets per row, and beta-binomial overdispersion ($\\phi=5$). Panel a): mean signed bias in $z$ (left column) and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ (right column) with 95% Monte Carlo uncertainty intervals (mean ± 1.96 MCSE). Panel b): 95% interval coverage with the same column layout. Dashed lines mark zero bias and nominal coverage. Two-stage Normal- and t-quantile variants share point estimates and differ only in Stage-2 delta-method interval construction. 4PL = four-parameter log-logistic, BB = beta-binomial, bin = binomial, CI = 95% interval (credible interval for the 4PL, confidence interval for the two-stage approaches)."

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(patchwork)

# ---- Method ordering + paired colour palette (matches notes writeup) --
.method_levels <- c("two_stage_bin", "two_stage_bin_t",
                    "two_stage_bb",  "two_stage_bb_t",
                    "joint_4pl",     "joint_4pl_abs")
.method_labels <- c("Two-stage bin (Normal CI)", "Two-stage bin (t CI)",
                    "Two-stage BB (Normal CI)",  "Two-stage BB (t CI)",
                    "Joint 4PL (relative)",      "Joint 4PL (absolute)")
.method_cols <- setNames(c("#54278f","#cbc9e2","#a63603","#fdae6b",
                           "#006d2c","#a1d99b"), .method_labels)

# ---- Two-truth constants (mid line is fixed across all 25 sim cells) --
.TRUTH_REL <- c(z = -1 / -0.15,
                CTmax_1hr = 34 + (log10(60) - 1.5) / -0.15)

# ---- BB Stage-1 pathology screening + two-truth aggregation -----------
.load_screened <- function(prefix) {
  files <- list.files(
    here::here("output", "sim_twostage"),
    pattern = paste0("^per_sim_", prefix, "_.*[.]rds$"),
    full.names = TRUE)
  ps <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(files, readRDS))

  bad <- ps |>
    dplyr::filter(method == "two_stage_bb",
                  (quantity == "z"         & abs(bias) > 20) |
                  (quantity == "CTmax_1hr" & abs(bias) > 10)) |>
    dplyr::distinct(scenario, sim_id) |>
    dplyr::mutate(bb_path = TRUE)

  ps |>
    dplyr::left_join(bad, by = c("scenario", "sim_id")) |>
    dplyr::filter(is.na(bb_path) |
                  !(method %in% c("two_stage_bb", "two_stage_bb_t"))) |>
    dplyr::select(-bb_path) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      truth_use = ifelse(method == "joint_4pl",
                         .TRUTH_REL[as.character(quantity)],
                         truth),
      bias    = estimate - truth_use,
      covered = is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper) &
                lower <= truth_use & truth_use <= upper
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(success) |>
    dplyr::group_by(scenario, method, quantity) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      mean_bias = mean(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
      mcse_bias = stats::sd(bias, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
      coverage  = mean(covered, na.rm = TRUE),
      mcse_cov  = sqrt(mean(covered, na.rm = TRUE) *
                       (1 - mean(covered, na.rm = TRUE)) / dplyr::n()),
      .groups   = "drop"
    )
}

# Use n_reps = 5 cells of Scen 3 and Scen 5 for the manuscript figure.
.d <- dplyr::bind_rows(.load_screened("scen3"),
                       .load_screened("scen5")) |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("_n5$", scenario)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    method   = factor(method,   levels = .method_levels,
                                labels = .method_labels),
    quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("z", "CTmax_1hr"),
                                labels = c("z (°C)",
                                           "CT[max,1h] (°C)")),
    scenario_label = dplyr::recode(
      sub("_n5$", "", scenario),
      scen3_heat_lowers_u = "up varies with T",
      scen5_sharpen       = "k varies with T"),
    bias_lo = mean_bias - 1.96 * mcse_bias,
    bias_hi = mean_bias + 1.96 * mcse_bias,
    cov_lo  = coverage  - 1.96 * mcse_cov,
    cov_hi  = coverage  + 1.96 * mcse_cov
  )

.theme_proj <- theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        axis.title       = element_text(size = 13),
        axis.text        = element_text(size = 11),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.title     = element_blank(),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"))

.qlab2 <- as_labeller(c(`z (°C)` = "italic(z)~(degree*C)",
                        `CT[max,1h] (°C)` = "CT[max[1*hr]]~(degree*C)"), label_parsed)

.p_bias <- ggplot(.d, aes(x = mean_bias, y = method, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = bias_lo, xmax = bias_hi), height = 0.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(scenario_label ~ quantity, scales = "free_x", labeller = labeller(quantity = .qlab2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = .method_cols) +
  labs(x = "Mean bias (estimate - truth)", y = NULL,
       title = "a) Bias") +
  .theme_proj + theme(legend.position = "none")

.p_cov <- ggplot(.d, aes(x = coverage, y = method, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = cov_lo, xmax = cov_hi), height = 0.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(scenario_label ~ quantity, labeller = labeller(quantity = .qlab2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = .method_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 0.95)) +
  labs(x = "95% CI coverage", y = NULL,
       title = "b) Coverage") +
  .theme_proj

.p_bias / .p_cov + plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(1, 1)) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sims2

#| fig-cap: "Bias in $z$ and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ under two departures from a full upper asymptote. Panel a) (upper asymptote varies): $\\beta_{up} = 0$ (no temperature-dependent shift), but the upper asymptote is held at a reduced level across all temperatures, so the maximum attainable survival is lower throughout the grid. Panel b) (upper asymptote shifts with temperature): the upper asymptote at $T = \\bar T$ is fixed at $\\text{up}_0 = 0.92$ while its per-°C shift ($\\beta_{up}$) is varied, so $\\text{up}$ stays high at cool assays and declines progressively at hotter ones. Points are mean signed bias with 95% Monte Carlo uncertainty intervals (mean ± 1.96 MCSE); dashed lines mark zero bias. Left column: $z$; right column: $CT_{max_{1hr}}$. Only the four distinct point-estimate methods are shown: the two-stage Normal- and t-quantile variants share point estimates within each Stage-1 family, so bias is identical between them. Coverage differences are presented in the supplement for [panel a, Supplement 13.5](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#coverage-for-constant-but-reduced-up-textup_0) and [panel b, Supplement 13.4](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#coverage-for-shifting-up-across-temperatures-beta_up)."

library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# construction differs). For this bias-only figure we therefore plot

.method_levels <- c("two_stage_bin", "two_stage_bb",
                    "joint_4pl",     "joint_4pl_abs")
.method_labels <- c("Two-stage bin", "Two-stage BB",
                    "Joint 4PL (relative)", "Joint 4PL (absolute)")
.method_cols <- setNames(c("#54278f", "#a63603", "#006d2c", "#a1d99b"),
                         .method_labels)

# ---- Two-truth constants (mid line is fixed across all 25 sim cells) --
.TRUTH_REL <- c(z = -1 / -0.15,
                CTmax_1hr = 34 + (log10(60) - 1.5) / -0.15)

# ---- BB Stage-1 pathology screening + two-truth aggregation -----------
.load_screened <- function(prefix) {
  files <- list.files(
    here::here("output", "sim_twostage"),
    pattern = paste0("^per_sim_", prefix, "_.*[.]rds$"),
    full.names = TRUE)
  ps <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(files, readRDS))

  bad <- ps |>
    dplyr::filter(method == "two_stage_bb",
                  (quantity == "z"         & abs(bias) > 20) |
                  (quantity == "CTmax_1hr" & abs(bias) > 10)) |>
    dplyr::distinct(scenario, sim_id) |>
    dplyr::mutate(bb_path = TRUE)

  ps |>
    dplyr::left_join(bad, by = c("scenario", "sim_id")) |>
    dplyr::filter(is.na(bb_path) |
                  !(method %in% c("two_stage_bb", "two_stage_bb_t"))) |>
    dplyr::select(-bb_path) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      truth_use = ifelse(method == "joint_4pl",
                         .TRUTH_REL[as.character(quantity)],
                         truth),
      bias    = estimate - truth_use,
      covered = is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper) &
                lower <= truth_use & truth_use <= upper
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(success) |>
    dplyr::group_by(scenario, method, quantity) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      mean_bias = mean(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
      mcse_bias = stats::sd(bias, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
      .groups   = "drop"
    )
}

.scen6 <- .load_screened("scen6") |>
  dplyr::mutate(sweep_x = -as.numeric(sub("scen6_ub_m", "", scenario)) / 10,
                sweep_label = "up shifts with T (varying beta_up, percentage points / degC)")

.scen7 <- .load_screened("scen7") |>
  dplyr::mutate(sweep_x = as.numeric(sub("scen7_u0_", "", scenario)) / 100,
                sweep_label = "up is constant but reduced (varying up_0)")

.shape_fmt <- function(d) {
  d |>
    dplyr::filter(method %in% .method_levels) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      method   = factor(method,   levels = .method_levels,
                                  labels = .method_labels),
      quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("z", "CTmax_1hr"),
                                  labels = c("z (°C)",
                                             "CT[max,1h] (°C)")),
      bias_lo = mean_bias - 1.96 * mcse_bias,
      bias_hi = mean_bias + 1.96 * mcse_bias
    )
}

.theme_proj <- theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        axis.title       = element_text(size = 13),
        axis.text        = element_text(size = 11),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.title     = element_blank(),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"))

.qlab2 <- as_labeller(c(`z (°C)` = "italic(z)~(degree*C)",
                        `CT[max,1h] (°C)` = "CT[max[1*hr]]~(degree*C)"), label_parsed)

.build <- function(d, x_label, x_breaks) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x = sweep_x, y = mean_bias, colour = method)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = bias_lo, ymax = bias_hi), width = 0) +
    geom_point(size = 2.4) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1, labeller = .qlab2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = .method_cols) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = "Mean bias (estimate - truth)") +
    .theme_proj
}

.p6 <- .build(.shape_fmt(.scen6),
              x_label  = "Temperature-dependent shift in upper asymptote (percentage points/°C)",
              x_breaks = c(-1.9, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5)) +
  ggtitle("b) Upper asymptote shifts with temperature")

.p7 <- .build(.shape_fmt(.scen7),
              x_label  = "Upper asymptote value",
              x_breaks = c(0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95, 0.99)) +
  ggtitle("a) Upper asymptote varies")

.p7 / .p6 + plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(1, 1)) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-design
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Estimator performance across experimental designs. Panels a) and b) vary experimental design and replication: a full (5 temperatures × 6 durations) versus sparse (3 × 4) temperature–duration grid, crossed with 1, 3, or 5 replicate vials per treatment combination. Panels c) and d) vary the maximum exposure duration (the longest assay window: 60, 120, 240, or 405 min) on the full grid with five replicates. Panels a) and c) show mean signed bias and panels b) and d) show 95% interval coverage for thermal sensitivity $z$ (left) and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ (right). Points are Monte Carlo means with 95% Monte Carlo uncertainty intervals (mean ± 1.96 MCSE); dashed lines mark zero bias and nominal 0.95 coverage. Bias panels show the four distinct point estimators (the two-stage Normal- and *t*-CI variants share point estimates); coverage panels additionally distinguish the *t*-CI variants. All simulated scenarios use a beta-binomial data-generating process ($\\phi=5$) with a fixed 4PL shape ($\\text{up}=0.92$, $\\text{low}=0.05$, $k=8$, midpoint linear in $T$); $N_{sim}=1000$ datasets per simulated scenario. The simulated designs are drawn in Figures S30 and S32, and full scenario detail and RMSE are in [Supplement 13.6](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#experimental-design-impacts)."

# Combined experimental-design figure (scen8 = design × replication; scen9 =
# maximum exposure duration). Reads the per-simulation aggregates only — no
# model fits here. Mirrors the screening/aggregation used by the other
# simulation figures.
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(here); library(patchwork)

.method_levels <- c("two_stage_bin","two_stage_bin_t","two_stage_bb",
                    "two_stage_bb_t","joint_4pl","joint_4pl_abs")
.method_labels <- c("Two-stage bin (Normal CI)","Two-stage bin (t CI)",
                    "Two-stage BB (Normal CI)","Two-stage BB (t CI)",
                    "Joint 4PL (relative)","Joint 4PL (absolute)")
.method_cols <- setNames(c("#54278f","#cbc9e2","#a63603","#fdae6b",
                           "#006d2c","#a1d99b"), .method_labels)
.point_codes <- c("two_stage_bin","two_stage_bb","joint_4pl","joint_4pl_abs")
.TRUTH_REL   <- c(z = -1 / -0.15, CTmax_1hr = 34 + (log10(60) - 1.5) / -0.15)

.load_screened <- function(prefix) {
  files <- list.files(here::here("output","sim_twostage"),
                      pattern = paste0("^per_sim_", prefix, "_.*[.]rds$"),
                      full.names = TRUE)
  ps <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(files, readRDS))
  bad <- ps |>
    dplyr::filter(method == "two_stage_bb",
                  (quantity == "z" & abs(bias) > 20) |
                  (quantity == "CTmax_1hr" & abs(bias) > 10)) |>
    dplyr::distinct(scenario, sim_id) |> dplyr::mutate(bb_path = TRUE)
  ps |>
    dplyr::left_join(bad, by = c("scenario","sim_id")) |>
    dplyr::filter(is.na(bb_path) |
                  !(method %in% c("two_stage_bb","two_stage_bb_t"))) |>
    dplyr::select(-bb_path) |>
    dplyr::mutate(truth_use = ifelse(method == "joint_4pl",
                                     .TRUTH_REL[as.character(quantity)], truth),
                  bias = estimate - truth_use,
                  covered = is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper) &
                            lower <= truth_use & truth_use <= upper) |>
    dplyr::filter(success) |>
    dplyr::group_by(scenario, method, quantity) |>
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     mean_bias = mean(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
                     mcse_bias = stats::sd(bias, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
                     coverage  = mean(covered, na.rm = TRUE),
                     mcse_cov  = sqrt(mean(covered) * (1 - mean(covered)) / dplyr::n()),
                     .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(method_code = as.character(method))
}

.fmt <- function(d) d |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("z","CTmax_1hr"),
                      labels = c("z (°C)","CT[max,1h] (°C)")),
    method_lab = factor(.method_labels[match(method_code, .method_levels)],
                        levels = .method_labels),
    bias_lo = mean_bias - 1.96 * mcse_bias, bias_hi = mean_bias + 1.96 * mcse_bias,
    cov_lo  = coverage  - 1.96 * mcse_cov,  cov_hi  = coverage  + 1.96 * mcse_cov)

.d8 <- .fmt(.load_screened("scen8")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(design = ifelse(grepl("full", scenario), "full", "sparse"),
                nrep = as.integer(sub(".*_n([0-9]+)$", "\\1", scenario)),
                cell = factor(sprintf("%s × %d", design, nrep),
                              levels = rev(c("sparse × 1","full × 1","sparse × 3",
                                             "full × 3","sparse × 5","full × 5"))))
.d9 <- .fmt(.load_screened("scen9")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(tmax = as.integer(sub(".*_tmax_([0-9]+)$", "\\1", scenario)),
                cell = factor(sprintf("%d min", tmax),
                              levels = rev(c("60 min","120 min","240 min","405 min"))))

.qlab <- as_labeller(c(`z (°C)` = "italic(z)~(degree*C)",
                       `CT[max,1h] (°C)` = "CT[max[1*hr]]~(degree*C)"), label_parsed)
.thm <- theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12), axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.6, "lines"))
.scol <- scale_colour_manual(values = .method_cols, breaks = .method_labels,
                             limits = .method_labels, drop = FALSE)

.bias_panel <- function(d, title)
  ggplot(dplyr::filter(d, method_code %in% .point_codes),
         aes(mean_bias, cell, colour = method_lab, group = method_lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = bias_lo, xmax = bias_hi), height = .3,
                 position = position_dodge(.6)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, position = position_dodge(.6)) +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free_x", labeller = .qlab) +
  .scol + guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(x = "Mean bias (estimate - truth)", y = NULL, title = title) + .thm
.cov_panel <- function(d, title)
  ggplot(d, aes(coverage, cell, colour = method_lab, group = method_lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = cov_lo, xmax = cov_hi), height = .3,
                 position = position_dodge(.6)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, position = position_dodge(.6)) +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, labeller = .qlab) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, .5, .95)) +
  .scol + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                                       override.aes = list(size = 2.6))) +
  labs(x = "95% CI coverage", y = NULL, title = title) + .thm

.fig_design <-
  (.bias_panel(.d8, "a) Design × replication — bias") |
   .cov_panel(.d8,  "b) Design × replication — coverage")) /
  (.bias_panel(.d9, "c) Maximum exposure duration — bias") |
   .cov_panel(.d9,  "d) Maximum exposure duration — coverage")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")

dir.create(here::here("output","figs"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(here::here("output","figs","fig_sim_design.png"), .fig_design,
       width = 11, height = 10, dpi = 600, bg = "white")
ggsave(here::here("output","figs","fig_sim_design.svg"), .fig_design,
       width = 11, height = 10, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("output","figs","fig_sim_design.png"))
```

# Worked examples

We applied the 4PL modelling framework to four case studies spanning lethal counts, continuous-proportion physiological data and sublethal responses using four case studies: 1) three cereal-aphid species [@li2023], 2) snow gum leaf PSII function [@arnold_psii_2026], 3) zebrafish larvae under varying oxygen levels [@saruhashi2026] and 4) vinegar fly mortality, heat coma and productivity [@orsted_suzukii_2024]. These examples show how the same fitted response surface can estimate $z$, $CT_{max}$ and, for lethal endpoints, $T_{crit}$, compare groups, and propagate uncertainty into heat-injury and survival predictions. The workflow is implemented in `bayesTLS`; the online supplement provides installation instructions, a tutorial and the full model specifications ([Supplement Sections 1–4](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-general-intro)).

For the main grouped case studies, we used the direct parameterisation in @eq-empirical-direct, placing species, oxygen treatment or recovery condition directly on $CT_{max}$ and $z$. The vinegar-fly sex comparison was fit in the equivalent midpoint form, with `sex` and its temperature interaction on $\text{mid}$. Count responses were fit with beta-binomial likelihoods, while proportions in the snow gum example were fit with a beta likelihood, with zero readings treated as left-censored at the instrument's resolution. We fitted all models using a Bayesian implementation, with `brms` (v`r as.character(packageVersion("brms"))`; @burkner_brms_2017) and Stan (CmdStan v`r cmdstan_vers`; @carpenter2017) via `bayesTLS` (v`r as.character(packageVersion("bayesTLS"))`). Equivalent frequentist models are available via `freqTLS`, and we demonstrate their equivalence in [Supplement Section 16](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-freqtls).

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{mid}_{ij}(T) &= \log_{10} t_{\text{ref}} + \frac{CT_{max,ij}(t_{\text{ref}}) - T_{ij}}{z_{ij}},\\
CT_{max,ij}(t_{\text{ref}}) &= \alpha_0 + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha} + b_j,\\
\ln z_{ij} &= \zeta_0 + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\zeta} + u_j .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-empirical-direct}


For the lethal aphid and vinegar-fly examples, we also used posterior draws to predict heat injury and survival under field or field-derived temperature traces, with and without an illustrative Sharpe–Schoolfield temperature-dependent repair function [*sensu* @arnold_thermal_2025]. Model specifications are summarised in [Supplement Section 4](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-empirical-model-specs), with the exact calls (formulas, priors and sampler settings) and diagnostics given with each case study, and the repair model and temperature traces in [Supplement Section 15](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-ms-fig6). The survival estimates use posterior draws for $z$, $CT_{max_{1hr}}$, and $T_{crit}$ (estimated as the temperature at which injury starts to accumulate), linking laboratory tolerance to predictions of survival in the field.

```{r}
#| label: aphid-hi-facts
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Read cached aphid heat-injury facts, with fallbacks for independent rendering.
# Only trust a cache stamped by the authoritative supplement pipeline — an
# unstamped file (e.g. written by some ad-hoc script) falls through to the
# fallback values rather than silently feeding the text.
.f5 <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("output", "data", "fig5_hi_data.rds")),
                error = function(e) NULL)
.f5_fresh <- identical(.f5$provenance, "supplement.qmd") && !is.null(.f5$aphid_Tc)
# Summarise the per-species T_crit range (currently unused in the text; kept
# for convenience). Fallback matches the 2026-10-11 supplement render.
aphid_Tc_rng <- if (.f5_fresh) range(.f5$aphid_Tc$Tc) else c(23.2, 27.4)
# Summarise end-of-season survival without repair.
aphid_surv_end <- if (.f5_fresh) {
  .f5$aphid |>
    dplyr::filter(repair == "No repair") |>
    dplyr::group_by(species) |>
    dplyr::slice_max(time, n = 1) |>
    dplyr::pull(surv_med)
} else c(0.0200, 0.0212)
# Across-species survival as a percentage range. Rounding to whole percent was
# too coarse: the three species land at 2.00-2.12%, so min and max both printed
# as "2", giving the nonsensical "2-2%". Keep one decimal, and collapse to a
# single figure if the species do round to the same value.
aphid_surv_rng <- {
  .r <- round(100 * range(aphid_surv_end), 1)
  if (.r[1] == .r[2]) sprintf("%.1f", .r[1]) else sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", .r[1], .r[2])
}
```

## Cereal aphids (*Metopolophium dirhodum*, *Sitobion avenae*, *Rhopalosiphum padi*)

@li2023 found pronounced differences in heat tolerance and sensitivity among species, which likely explain changes in cereal-aphid communities. Our 4PL model recovers similar findings, with *R. padi* having the highest $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ = `r aphid_ct_rp` °C (exceeding *M. dirhodum* by `r ci1(cc$aphid_ct_rp_md)` °C, `r pmc(cc$aphid_ct_rp_md)`) and *M. dirhodum* the shallowest thermal-death-time slope (largest $z$ = `r aphid_z_md` °C) and the lowest $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ ([@fig-tls-comparison]a). However, because the 4PL is fit to the raw survival counts, its Bayesian $R^2$ was more realistic (`r aphid_r2[1]`, 95% CrI: `r aphid_r2[2]`–`r aphid_r2[3]`), and well below the $R^2$ values @li2023 reported for their two-stage regressions (0.97–0.99; [Supplement Section 7.3](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-aphid-extract)). 

Using field temperatures from the same site (Wuhan, China), we also show how the 4PL can predict field mortality with uncertainty propagated from that same model: survival without repair is predicted to fall to roughly `r aphid_surv_rng`% by late June, while physiological repair raised end-of-June survival by `r rep1(cc$aphid_repair$R_padi)` percentage points for *R. padi* and `r rep1(cc$aphid_repair$S_avenae)` for *S. avenae*, but barely changed it (`r rep1(cc$aphid_repair$M_dirhodum)` percentage points) for the least-tolerant *M. dirhodum* ([@fig-heat-injury]d-f). The model therefore moves inference from ranking laboratory tolerance to predicting which species is most likely to experience mortality during natural fluctuating temperature regimes.

## Snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*)

@arnold_psii_2026 showed that light conditions alter estimates of heat damage to photosystem II (PSII), an ecologically important endpoint because the leaves of snow gum (and most other canopy-forming plants) experience the most extreme heat during daylight, often with high solar input. We fitted a 4PL model to continuous PSII proportions (post/pre $F_v/F_m$) with a beta distribution, treating zero readings as below the instrument's resolution (left-censored) and modelling the experiment's split-plot design: light or dark recovery was applied to whole arrays of leaf sections, so arrays, not sections, replicate the treatment. With arrays as the unit of replication, light recovery changed $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ by `r ci1(cc$sg_ct)` °C (`r pmc(cc$sg_ct)`) and $z$ by `r ci1(cc$sg_z)` °C (`r pmc(cc$sg_z)`; [@fig-tls-comparison]b) relative to dark recovery. Both are lower under light (for $CT_{max}$, as @arnold_psii_2026 found), but these data do not resolve either difference once variation among arrays is accounted for ([Supplement Section 8](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-leaves)). 

## Zebrafish (*Danio rerio*)

@saruhashi2026 found that oxygen modulates heat tolerance in zebrafish larvae, an important result because freshwater heatwaves often coincide with changing oxygen availability. Despite the sparse design, which would make it challenging to use a two-stage analysis to estimate $CT_{max}$ and $z$, we show that the 4PL can still be used. Hyperoxia steepened the TDT relationship relative to normoxia ($\Delta z$ = `r ci1(cc$zf_z)` °C, `r pmc(cc$zf_z)`; [@fig-tls-comparison]c). $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ was higher under hyperoxia (`r zf_ct_hyper_ci` vs `r zf_ct_norm_ci` °C), as @saruhashi2026 found, but the difference was not significant ($\Delta CT_{max_{1hr}}$ = `r ci1(cc$zf_ct)` °C, `r pmc(cc$zf_ct)`). Oxygen therefore changes how fast injury accumulates during heat stress, so its benefit depends on exposure duration as well as temperature.

## Vinegar fly (*Drosophila suzukii*)

@orsted_suzukii_2024 found that heat coma and declines in productivity occur at temperatures below survival limits but follow traditional TDT relationships, implying that sublethal effects have large implications for population dynamics. Our re-analysis of their survival data recovers similar variation in thermal tolerance and sensitivity between sexes ($z$ = `r fly_z_f_ci` °C for females and `r fly_z_m_ci` °C for males; $CT_{max_{4hr}}$ ≈ `r fly_ct_4h` °C; [@fig-tls-comparison]d), but estimates the sex contrast directly in a unified model and finds no detectable difference. Males had a slightly higher $z$ than females ($\Delta z$ = `r ci1(cc$fly_z)` °C, `r pmc(cc$fly_z)`) and an almost identical $CT_{max_{4hr}}$ ($\Delta CT_{max_{4hr}}$ = `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", cc$fly_ct["med"], cc$fly_ct["lo"], cc$fly_ct["hi"])` °C, `r pmc(cc$fly_ct)`). As with the aphids, retaining the raw-response variance gives more realistic fit summaries (Bayesian $R^2$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", cc$fly_r2["Female"])` for females and `r sprintf("%.2f", cc$fly_r2["Male"])` for males; [Supplement Table S19](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#tbl-r2-dros)). In the supplement, we also extend modelling approach to heat coma ([Supplement Section 10.1](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-dros-coma)) and productivity ([Supplement Section 10.2](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-dros-productivity)), including a hurdle model that separates reproductive failure from changes in offspring number among reproducing flies. 

We generated predictions on heat injury and predicted mortality using a microclimate temperature-time series for Rennes, France. Such modelling illustrates how patterns of population mortality for both sexes can be predicted in nature with and without repair ([@fig-heat-injury]a-c), showing how repair (even at small rates) can have important population-level consequences.

# Discussion

In this study, we show that conventional TDT/TLS analyses can be reparameterised using a four-parameter log-logistic model (4PL) to offer more robust, accurate, and generalisable predictions of the impacts of extreme heat on organisms. While simplified models or even other dose-response models can be used, the 4PL model provides a flexible and statistically rigorous framework for estimating thermal tolerance and thermal sensitivity, recovering familiar quantities such as $z$ and $CT_{max}$. At the same time, the model derives estimates from the full temperature-duration response surface and propagates uncertainty into every derived quantity. Simulations show that the joint model reproduces classical estimates when two-stage assumptions hold, but is more reliable when experiments are sparse, replication is low, exposure windows are short, or the response bounds (`low`, `up`) depart from 0 and 1 (@fig-sims–@fig-sim-design). Using four case studies across diverse plant and animal taxa, we show how the model recovers biologically plausible TLS estimates, with $z$ values falling within the range typically reported for thermal tolerance landscapes (approximately 2-7 °C; @rezende_landscapes_2014), and unlocks opportunities to extend inference to sublethal endpoints, group contrasts, and survival under fluctuating temperature regimes.

One of the key challenges in global change biology is to understand the ecological and evolutionary drivers of thermal sensitivity and tolerance across life [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @jorgensen_nature_2022]. Species, populations, life stages, and organisms exposed to various experimental treatments are likely to differ in the temperature at which damage starts to accumulate ($T_{crit}$), the rate at which damage accumulates ($z$), and how much heat load they can endure ($CT_{max}$) [@arnold_thermal_2025; @li2023; @orsted_suzukii_2024; @saruhashi2026; @youngblood2025]. We need robust statistical approaches that allow us to quantify differences in how temperatures impact biological function, which was not previously possible with conventional two-stage analysis pipelines. Using broad case studies, we illustrate the power of our modelling approach in estimating these parameters and how they differ among groups of particular interest in global change biology. In cereal aphids, our model was able to statistically compare differences in thermal tolerance and sensitivity among species, and to link interspecific differences in heat tolerance measured in the laboratory to predicted survival under natural temperature regimes. In the snow gum, the model showed that whether post-heat light appears to lower PSII heat tolerance depends on treating the arrays, to which light was applied, as the replicates. When these sources of non-independence were accounted for, despite $CT_{max}$ and $z$ both being lower under light (by `r sprintf("%.1f", -cc$sg_ct["med"])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", -cc$sg_z["med"])` °C), neither difference was significant. In zebrafish, oxygen changed how quickly tolerance time falls with warming ($z$), while its effect on $CT_{max}$ (`r sprintf("%.1f", cc$zf_ct["med"])` °C higher under hyperoxia) was ambiguous. In vinegar flies, we show that the sexes respond similarly to heat stress (males' $z$ and $CT_{max_{4hr}}$ were `r sprintf("%.1f", cc$fly_z["med"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", cc$fly_ct["med"])` °C higher than females', with the difference being non-significant), but that vital rates (i.e., mortality, coma, productivity) follow distinct thermal tolerance landscapes and fail at different temperatures under extreme heat. These ecological inferences provide new insights into the mechanisms that may underlie vulnerability to extreme heat, not only alternative ways for estimating $z$ or $CT_{max}$.

Because the 4PL model fits raw response data in a single hierarchical analysis, it also creates new opportunities for asking where variation in responses comes from. Clones, individuals, tissues, sexes, populations, or treatments can be included in the same model, on any of the 4PL parameters, to estimate genetic, individual, tissue-specific, and environmental sources of variance in $z$ and $CT_{max}$. The posterior distributions of the underlying 4PL parameters (`low`, `up`, `k`, and `mid`) can also be contrasted to determine whether groups differ in baseline survival, maximum attainable survival, curve steepness or thermal sensitivity. This kind of variance decomposition is not possible with a two-stage pipeline because the first stage collapses the response surface to a small set of point estimates, and the second stage treats those estimates as data. Full propagation of sampling uncertainty should also make tolerance and sensitivity estimates more useful, and less biased, for robust meta-analyses, comparative studies, and systems models of biological responses to extreme heat [@noble2026; @pottier2024].

The same modelling framework extends beyond lethal count data to many sublethal measures that are of interest to ecologists and evolutionary biologists and could arguably be more important in assessing vulnerability to environmental change [@arnold_psii_2026; @bretman2024; @orsted2026; @snook_fertility_2026]. In the supplement, we show how derivatives of the 4PL model can be used for time-to-event responses, mixture models that separate response and non-response components, Gamma-distributed responses, and continuous proportions. This modelling framework can also be expanded to include interacting stressors (e.g., oxygen, acidification, pollutants), as well as temperature-dependent effects on acclimation, physiological repair, and behaviour, which can all modulate the accumulation of heat injury under fluctuating temperature regimes [@arnold_thermal_2025]. More generally, any dose-response process in which biological responses depend jointly on stress intensity and exposure duration could be analysed with this framework, including toxicology studies where toxicant concentration replaces temperature. Therefore, the 4PL modelling framework opens avenues to build greater consistency in reporting and analytical choices across fields, which can have consequences for ecological inference [@gould2025].

While the 4PL framework is powerful, it also has limitations. Fitting models with temperature-dependent effects on all parameters may cause some to be estimated poorly in very small datasets. However, our simulations show that, even with small sample sizes and less rigorous designs, the 4PL can recover correctly calibrated estimates, which offers opportunities to apply this framework to taxa where large sample sizes are difficult to achieve. Nonetheless, models may at times need to be simplified, for example by ignoring temperature-dependent shifts in `up`, `low`, or `k` if they are not well supported by the data. We provide capacity to simplify models when needed in `bayesTLS` by allowing `up` and `low` to be fixed when needed. In fact, multiple models (including different dose-response models) can be fit to the data and their fit evaluated with WAIC or LOO model comparison ([Supplement Section 11](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-curve-comparison)). Sampling diagnostics also show when a parameter is poorly estimated. For example, each parameter should have $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 400, which `diagnose_tdt_fit()` checks. If a parameter (e.g., a temperature effect on `k` or `up`) fails these checks, longer chains with a longer warm-up can help. If they do not, the parameter can be fixed or dropped from the model. Bayesian implementations also require priors that are appropriate for the biological system, although `bayesTLS` is designed to make these models more accessible to experimental and comparative biologists. We provide a prior sensitivity check ([Supplement Section 12](https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/#sec-prior-sensitivity)), but show $CT_{max}$ and $z$ are minimally affected unless priors are too strong and data is minimal. Similar models can also be fitted in a likelihood framework, with uncertainty propagated using profiled likelihood, parametric bootstrapping or the Delta method [@bolker_ecologicalmodels_2008]. We provide this option through `freqTLS`. However, propagating uncertainty into survival and heat-injury predictions is more straightforward within the Bayesian framework, which also incorporates prior information. These predictions come with credible intervals that can help inform decisions, for example by giving the probability that survival under a given temperature regime falls below a threshold of concern, or by showing where intervals are too wide to act on and more data are needed. A major next step is to estimate repair parameters directly from experiments [@arnold_thermal_2025; @buckley_damage_2025; @orsted2026], because our illustrative Sharpe–Schoolfield repair model (*sensu* @arnold_thermal_2025) shows that predictions of mortality can change substantially when repair is included. Future models that combine heat injury, repair, acclimation, behaviour, and microclimate validation will be essential for translating laboratory tolerance surfaces into robust forecasts of survival in nature [@arnold_psii_2026; @faber2026a; @noble2026].

Taken together, our joint modelling framework allows more flexible, robust, and generalisable inferences of thermal tolerance, sensitivity, and vulnerability of organisms to extreme heat. This framework not only helps us better understand the ecological and evolutionary drivers of biological responses within and among species, but also helps translate laboratory estimates into uncertainty-aware forecasts of survival under fluctuating temperature regimes in the field. Therefore, this modelling framework is likely to improve our ability to predict organisms' vulnerability to increasingly intense, frequent, and long-lasting extreme heat events that will be common in the future.

# Data and code availability {.unnumbered}

Analysis code and case-study data are available at https://github.com/daniel1noble/bayesTLS, which is both the `bayesTLS` package repository and the research compendium for this paper. The four case-study datasets are included with the package as documented data objects (`aphid_tdt`, `dsuzukii`, `snowgum_psii`, `zebrafish_o2`); raw source files and temperature traces are in `inst/extdata/`, and the scripts that build the data objects and traces are in `data-raw/`. The full case-study analyses are in `ms/supplement.qmd` and rendered at https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/. The simulation is run by `scripts/simulations/run_simulations.R`. Stored simulation outputs and model fits are archived on OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/C6DXY) and fetched with `make data`. The sister package `freqTLS` (https://github.com/itchyshin/freqTLS) develops the same log-logistic models in a likelihood framework.
